Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 9, verse 1:

It is also called Surat al-Tawba (the Chapter of Repentance), and it is also called al-Fadiha (the Disgracing Chapter), because it exposed the secrets of the hypocrites. The codices and the reciters agree on omitting the basmala (the formula "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful") from its beginning, and there is disagreement about the reason for this. ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan said: its meanings resembled the meanings of al-Anfal, and it was called "the two companions" (al-qarinatayn) in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he joined the two and placed them among the seven long surahs. The Companions had also disagreed over whether the two were two surahs or one surah, so the basmala was left out between them for this reason. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib said: the basmala is a pledge of security, and Bara'a was revealed with the sword, so it did not begin with the pledge of security. ﴿A declaration of immunity from Allah and His Messenger﴾. The intended meaning of al-bara'a (immunity/disavowal) is the disavowal of the polytheists. The word bara'a is in the nominative either as the predicate of an implied subject or as the subject of an implied predicate. ﴿To those with whom you made a treaty among the polytheists﴾. The sense of the sentence is: a declaration coming from Allah and His Messenger to those with whom you made a treaty among the polytheists. Here "min" and "ila" are linked to an implied element, not to bara'a. The treaty is attributed to the Muslims in His saying "you made a treaty" because the action of the Prophet (ﷺ) is binding upon the Muslims, so it is as if they were the ones who made the treaty with the polytheists. The Prophet (ﷺ) had made treaties with the polytheists for specified terms; some of them fulfilled their obligations, so Allah commanded that his treaty with them be completed until its term, while others broke it or came close to breaking it, so a period of four months was granted to them, and after that they would have no treaty.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 9, verse 2:

﴿So travel freely through the land for four months﴾. That is, travel in safety for four months, which is the term that was set for them. Scholars differed about when these months were. It was said: they are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah and al-Muharram, because the surah was revealed at that time, which was the year nine (of the Hijrah). It was also said: they run from the Day of Eid al-Adha to the completion of the first ten days of Rabi' al-Akhir, because they only came to know of this at that time. That is because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Abu Bakr al-Siddiq that year to lead the people in Hajj, and then sent after him 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who recited Surah Bara'ah (al-Tawbah) to the people on the Day of 'Arafah. It was also said: on the Day of Sacrifice (al-Nahr). ﴿Know that you cannot escape Allah﴾. That is, you cannot elude Him.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 9, verse 3:

﴿وَأَذَٰنٌ﴾ means announcement (i'lam) of the disavowal of Allah the Exalted and His Messenger from the polytheists. ﴿إِلَى ٱلنَّاسِ﴾ — He made the disavowal specific to those polytheists who had a treaty (mu'ahadin), and made the announcement of the disavowal general for all people: those who had a treaty and those who did not, and the polytheists and others. ﴿ٱلْحَجِّ ٱلأَكْبَرِ﴾ is the Day of 'Arafah or the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr). It is said: the days of the season (al-mawsim) all of them. It was expressed by "a day," as you say "the day of Siffin and the Camel," although they were many days. ﴿أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ بَرِيۤءٌ مِّنَ ٱلْمُشْرِكِينَ﴾ — its estimated form is "an announcement that Allah is disavowing," and the preposition "bi" was omitted for lightness. It is also read as "inna Allaha" with a kasra, because the announcement (adhan) carries the meaning of saying (qawl). ﴿وَرَسُولُهُ﴾ is in the nominative by coordination with the pronoun in "bari'" (barī'), or by coordination with the position of the subject of "inna" (the noun of inna), or it is in the nominative as a beginning (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted. It is also read in the accusative, coordinated with the noun of "inna." As for the genitive, coordination with "al-mushrikin" is not permissible, because it is a corrupt meaning. It is permissible by way of proximity (al-jiwar) or by oath, but this is far-fetched, and the reading with it is irregular (shadhdhah). ﴿فَإِن تُبْتُمْ﴾ means repentance from disbelief (al-tawbah min al-kufr).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 9, verses 4–5:

﴿Except those with whom you made a treaty﴾: he means those who did not break the covenant. ﴿Then when the sacred months have passed﴾: he means the four months that were granted to them. Whoever says they are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah and Muharram, which are the well-known sacred months, [holds that] Shawwal was added and Rajab was dropped, and they were called sacred (ḥurum) by way of prevailing the majority. And whoever says they run until Rabi' al-Thani, [holds that] they were called sacred for their sanctity and for the prohibition of fighting in them at that time. ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾: it abrogates every truce mentioned in the Qur'an (naskh, abrogation). It is also said that it was itself abrogated, so that either release (manna) or ransom (fida') follows. It is also said: rather, it abrogated those (rulings), so that release and ransom are permissible. ﴿And seize them﴾: its meaning is capture, and the akhidh (ukhidh) is the captive. ﴿And lie in wait for them at every place of ambush﴾: every path; it is in the accusative as an adverb of place (ẓarf). ﴿But if they repent﴾: he means from disbelief. Then he joined with faith the prayer and the zakat, and this is evidence for fighting those who abandon prayer and zakat, as Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) did. The verse is in the sense of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I have been commanded to fight the people until they say, 'There is no god but Allah,' and establish the prayer and give the zakat." ﴿Then let them go their way﴾: a guarantee of safety for them.

And if any of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection (﴿وَإِنْ أَحَدٌ مِّنَ ٱلْمُشْرِكِينَ ٱسْتَجَارَكَ فَأَجِرْهُ﴾). This ruling is established according to some scholars, but others said that it was abrogated (naskh, the replacement of a ruling by a later one) by fighting.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 9, verse 7–13:

﴿How can there be a covenant for the polytheists﴾ The interrogative particle (kayfa, "how") here carries the sense of disapproval and improbability. ﴿except for those with whom you made a covenant at al-Masjid al-Haram﴾ It has been said that the intended people are the Quraysh, and it has been said that they are the tribes of Banu Bakr. ﴿So long as they remain upright toward you﴾ Here "ma" (mā) is temporal (ẓarfiyyah). ﴿how﴾ is an emphatic repetition of the first (kayfa), and the verb after it has been omitted because it is understood; its estimated form is: "How can there be a covenant for them?" ﴿they do not observe﴾ meaning they do not respect ﴿regarding a relative or a pact.﴾ The term "il" means kinship; it has also been said that it means an alliance, while "dhimmah" means covenant. ﴿And most of them are defiantly disobedient.﴾ He excepted those for whom faith was decreed. ﴿the leaders of disbelief﴾ meaning the chiefs of its people. It has been said that they are Abu Jahl, may Allah curse him, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, and Suhayl ibn Amr; al-Tabari related this, but it is weak, because most of these had died before the revelation of this surah. The better view is that the verse is general. ﴿for them there are no oaths﴾ meaning they have no oaths that they keep. It has been read as "la iymana" with a kasra on the hamzah. ﴿so that they may desist﴾ This is connected to "qatilu" (fight). ﴿And they plotted to expel the Messenger﴾ It has been said that this means expelling him from Madinah when they fought him at the Trench and at Uhud; and it has been said that it means expelling him from Makkah, when they consulted about it in the Dar al-Nadwah, after which he himself departed. ﴿And they began the first attack against you﴾ meaning: their harming of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims in Makkah.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 9, verse 16:

﴿Or did you think﴾ The verse means that Allah will not leave them without a testing (tamhis) through which the good is distinguished from the wicked. Here "am" (أم) carries the sense of "bal" (بل, "rather") together with the interrogative hamza. ﴿Allah knows﴾ That is: He knows this in a way that makes it a binding proof against them. ﴿Walijah (وليجة)﴾ That is, an intimate confidant (bitanah).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 9, verses 17–20:

﴿It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of God﴾. That is, it is not right or proper for them to do so, even though they have maintained them through dominance and injustice. Whoever reads *masajid* (مساجد) in the plural intends all the mosques, and whoever reads it in the singular (*bi-l-tawhid*) intends the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram).

﴿bearing witness against themselves to disbelief﴾. That is, their states and their statements require them to acknowledge disbelief. It has also been said that this refers to their saying in the *talbiyah* (the pilgrim's chant): "There is no partner for You, except a partner who belongs to You."

﴿Have you made the providing of water for the pilgrims...﴾ The verse. Its occasion of revelation was that a group from Quraysh boasted about providing water for the pilgrims and about maintaining the Sacred Mosque. So God made clear that jihad is better than that. The verse was revealed concerning Ali ibn Abi Talib, al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib and Talhah ibn Shaybah, who boasted. Talhah said: "I am the keeper of the House, and I hold its keys." Al-Abbas said: "I am the keeper of the water-providing." Ali said: "I embraced Islam before the people, and I fought alongside the Messenger of God (ﷺ)."

"And the Day of Hunayn" is either conjoined with "the battlefields" (mawatin) or governed by a verb understood (mudmar). The second is better, for two reasons. First, His words "when your great number pleased you" apply specifically to Hunayn and not to the other battlefields, so conjoining "the Day of Hunayn" to "the battlefields" becomes weak because of the difference between them in this respect. Second, "battlefields" (mawatin) is a noun of place, whereas "the Day of Hunayn" is a noun of time, so conjoining one to the other is weak, unless by "battlefields" one means "times."

Hunayn is a proper noun for a place, named after a man called Hunayn, and it is treated as diptote (inṣarafa) because it is masculine. "When your great number pleased you" (idh a'jabatkum kathratukum): on that day they were twelve thousand. Some of them said, "We will not be defeated today for lack of numbers." So God willed to show their weakness, and the people fled from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), until only he remained on his white mule with a small group. Then he sought help from God, took a handful of dust, threw it at the faces of the disbelievers, and said, "May the faces be disfigured." He called out to his companions, and they returned to him, and God defeated the disbelievers. The story of Hunayn is recorded in the biographies (al-siyar).

"With all its vastness" (bima rahubat): that is, it became constricted for you despite its great expanse. Here "ma" is a verbal-masdar particle (masdariyya).

"Then God turns" (thumma yatubu Allah): an indication of the conversion to Islam of the Hawazin, who fought the Muslims at Hunayn.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 9, verse 28:

﴿Truly the polytheists are impure﴾. It has been said: their impurity is due to their disbelief. And it has been said: it is due to ritual impurity (janabah). ﴿So let them not approach the Sacred Mosque﴾. This is an explicit text prohibiting the polytheists, who are idol-worshippers, from the Sacred Mosque, so the scholars unanimously agreed upon this. Malik analogized from the polytheists to all disbelievers, from the People of the Book and others, and he analogized from the Sacred Mosque to all other mosques, so he prohibited all disbelievers from all mosques. Al-Shafi'i took it as general regarding disbelievers but specific to the Sacred Mosque, so he prohibited all disbelievers from entering the Sacred Mosque specifically, and permitted them to enter other than it. Abu Hanifa restricted it to the place of the explicit text; so he prohibited the polytheists specifically from entering the Sacred Mosque specifically, and permitted them to enter all other mosques, and he permitted the People of the Book to enter the Sacred Mosque and other than it. ﴿After this their year﴾. He means the ninth year after the Hijrah, when Abu Bakr performed the Hajj with the people, and 'Ali recited to them Surah Bara'ah. ﴿And if you fear poverty﴾, that is, destitution. The polytheists used to bring foodstuffs to Makkah, so the people feared scarcity of provisions there once the polytheists were prevented from it. So Allah promised them that He would enrich them from His bounty, and all the Arabs embraced Islam, the importing of foodstuffs to Makkah continued, and then Allah opened all the regions.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 9, verse 29:

﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah and nor in the Last Day⁠—﴾ He commanded fighting against the People of the Book, and denied that they have faith in Allah, because of the saying of the Jews, "Uzayr is the son of Allah," and the saying of the Christians, "The Messiah is the son of Allah." He also denied that they have faith in the Last Day, because their belief concerning it is corrupt, for they do not affirm the Resurrection and the Reckoning. ﴿And who do not consider unlawful what Allah and His Messenger have made unlawful﴾, because they treat as lawful carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and other things. ﴿Nor adopt the religion of truth﴾, i.e., they do not enter Islam. ﴿From among those who were given the Scripture﴾ is an explanation of those whom He commanded to be fought. When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out on the expedition of Tabuk to fight the Christians. ﴿Until they give the jizyah﴾ The scholars agreed on accepting the jizyah (poll tax) from Jews and Christians, and the Magians are joined to them, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Treat them as you treat the People of the Book." They differed concerning accepting it from idol-worshippers and the Sabians. It is not taken from women, children, or the insane. According to Malik, its amount is four dinars on the people of gold, and forty dirhams on the people of silver, and it is taken from every head. ﴿With willing submission (ʿan yadin)﴾ Regarding this there are two interpretations: the first is that the dhimmi hands it over with his own hand, not sending it with anyone else, and not delaying it, as in the expression "hand to hand" (yadan bi-yad). The second is that it means with submission and compliance, as in your saying: "So-and-so cast his hand," i.e., surrendered. ﴿And they are humbled﴾, i.e., humiliated.

﴿And the Jews said, "’Uzayr is the son of Allah."﴾ Ibn ‘Abbas said: This statement was made by four of the Jews: Salam ibn Mishkam, Nu‘man ibn Awfa, Shas ibn Qays, and Malik ibn al-Sayf. It is also said that only Finhas said it, and it was attributed to all of them because they follow the one who said it. The apparent meaning is that their whole community said it, since they did not deny it when it was attributed to them. The reason for their saying this was that they lost the Torah, and ‘Uzayr alone had memorised it, so he taught it to them. They said: "Allah taught ‘Uzayr the Torah only because he is His son." ‘Uzayr is the subject (mubtada’), and "son of Allah" is the predicate (khabar). ‘Uzayr is not given tanwin (nunation) because it is foreign (a‘jami) and non-declinable (la yanṣarif) in grammar. It is also said: "Rather, it is declinable, and the tanwin was dropped because of the meeting of two unvocalised letters." But this view is weak. As for the one who gives it tanwin, he treats it as Arabic.

﴿And the Christians said, "The Messiah is the son of Allah."﴾

Abu al-Ma‘ali said: The Christians have unanimously agreed that the Messiah is God and the son of God, and that is a monstrous disbelief.

﴿with their mouths﴾ contains two meanings. The first is to hold them to this statement and to emphasise it. The second is that they have no proof for it; it is merely an assertion, like your saying to someone whom you accuse of lying: "This is a statement of your tongue."

﴿They imitate the saying of those who disbelieved before﴾. The meaning of yudahi’un is yushabihun (they resemble). If the pronoun refers to the Jews and Christians, then the words "those who disbelieved before" refer to the polytheists of the Arabs, who said, "The angels are daughters of Allah," and they were the first disbelievers. Or it refers to the Sabians, or to earlier nations. If the pronoun refers to the Jews and Christians contemporary with the Prophet (ﷺ), then "those who disbelieved before" are their earlier predecessors.

﴿May Allah destroy them﴾ is an invocation against them. It is also said that it means: "May Allah curse them."

﴿How are they turned away?﴾ is an expression of wonder: how they are diverted from truth and rightness.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 9, verse 31:

﴿They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah﴾ That is, they obeyed them as one obeys the Lord, even though they did not worship them. ﴿And the Messiah﴾ is conjoined with "the rabbis and the monks." ﴿Yet they were not commanded except to worship one God⁠—﴾ That is, Jesus and Muhammad (ﷺ) commanded them to do so.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 9, verses 32–33:

﴿They wish to extinguish the light of Allah﴾ meaning: they wish to extinguish the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and what he brought of worshipping Allah and affirming His oneness. ﴿With their mouths﴾ is an indication of their statements, such as their saying "a sorcerer" and "a poet." It also indicates the weakness of their scheming regarding what they intended. ﴿But Allah will not allow except that He perfect His light.﴾ ﴿That He may make it prevail over all religion﴾: the pronoun refers either to the Messenger (ﷺ) or to the religion. Making it prevail means making it the highest and strongest of the religions, so that it covers the easts and the wests. It was said that this will occur at the descent of ʿIsā ibn Maryam, so that nothing remains but the religion of Islam.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 9, verses 36–37:

﴿اثْنَا عَشَرَ شَهْراً﴾ are the well-known months, the first of which is al-Muharram and the last of which is Dhu al-Hijjah. It was ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (رضي الله عنه) who made al-Muharram the first month of the year.

﴿فِي كِتَابِ اللَّهِ﴾ means: in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). It is also said: in the Qur'an, but the first view is more preferred, because of His saying: ﴿on the day He created the heavens and the earth﴾.

﴿مِنْهَا أَرْبَعَةٌ حُرُمٌ﴾ are Rajab, Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah and al-Muharram.

﴿ذَلِكَ الدِّينُ الْقَيِّمُ﴾ means that the sanctity of the forbidden months is the upright religion, the religion of Ibrahim and Isma'il. The Arabs had held fast to it, until some of them changed it.

﴿فَلَا تَظْلِمُوا فِيهِنَّ أَنْفُسَكُمْ﴾: the pronoun in His saying ﴿فِيهِنَّ﴾ refers to the sacred months, to magnify their matter and to make sins in them more grave, even though wrongdoing is prohibited in other times. It is also said that the pronoun refers to the twelve months, or to all of time, but the first is more apparent.

﴿وَقَاتِلُوا الْمُشْرِكِينَ كَافَّةً﴾ means: fight them in the sacred months. This is an abrogation (naskh) of the prohibition of fighting in them. ﻿كَافَّةً (kaffatan, "all together") is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) referring either to the doer or to the object.

﴿إِنَّمَا النَّسِيءُ﴾ (al-nasi', "intercalation") is the postponement of the sanctity of one month to another month. The reason is that the Arabs were people of warfare and raids, and fighting was forbidden to them in the sacred months, so it was hard for them to abandon it. They would therefore make it in a forbidden month and declare another month sacred in its place. Sometimes they would make al-Muharram permissible and declare Safar forbidden, until there were four forbidden months completed in the year.

﴿يُحِلُّونَهُ عَاماً وَيُحَرِّمُونَهُ عَاماً﴾ means: sometimes they make it lawful and sometimes they make it forbidden. The word "year" is not meant literally.

﴿لِيُوَاطِئُوا عِدَّةَ مَا حَرَّمَ اللَّهُ﴾ means: their making fighting lawful in the sacred months.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 9, verse 40:

﴿Unless you help him, Allah has already helped him﴾ is a conditional clause (shart) with its response (jawab), and the pronoun refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 9, verses 41–42:

﴿Go forth, light and heavy﴾. This is a command to go out to military campaign (nafir ila al-ghazw). "Light" (al-khaffah) is used figuratively for one who is able to travel with ease, and "heavy" (al-thiql) for one who is able to do so only with difficulty. Some scholars said: the "light" is the wealthy, and the "heavy" is the poor. It was also said: the "light" is the young man, and the "heavy" is the elderly. And it was said: the "light" is the energetic, and the "heavy" is the lazy. These sayings are examples of heaviness and lightness. It was also said that this verse is abrogated (mansukhah) by His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon the weak or upon the sick﴾ [al-Tawbah: 91], and so on. ﴿Had it been a near gain﴾, and so on: it was revealed, along with much of what follows it in this surah, concerning the hypocrites who stayed behind from the expedition of Tabuk. That is because it was toward a distant land, in intense heat, with ripe fruits and shade, and so it weighed heavily upon them. Some scholars said: the "light" is the wealthy, and the "heavy" is the poor. It was also said: the "light" is the young man, and the "heavy" is the elderly. And it was said: the "light" is the energetic, and the "heavy" is the lazy. These sayings are examples of heaviness and lightness. It was also said that this verse is abrogated (mansukhah) by His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon the weak or upon the sick﴾ [al-Tawbah: 91], and so on. ﴿Had it been a near gain﴾, and so on: it was revealed, along with much of what follows it in this surah, concerning the hypocrites who stayed behind from the expedition of Tabuk. ʿAfā Allāh ʿanka li-ma adhinta lahum (ﷺ)... Let me translate carefully.

"God pardon you (ʿafā Allāh ʿanka); why did you give them leave?" — the verse. Some of the hypocrites had asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for permission to remain behind from the expedition to Tabuk, and he granted them leave. So God rebuked him for his granting them leave, and He placed the pardon before the rebuke, out of honour for him (ﷺ). It is said: his words "God pardon you" are not for a sin or a rebuke, but are an opening phrase of speech, as one says "May God set you right."

"Until those who are truthful become clear to you, and you know the liars." They had said: "Let us ask him for permission to stay behind; if he gives us leave, we will stay behind, and if he does not give us leave, we will stay behind." ﴿Alms are only for the poor and the needy﴾ (verse). Here "innama" (only) indicates a restriction of the ṣadaqāt, which means the zakat (obligatory alms), to these eight categories. It is not permissible to give any of it to anyone else. The position of Mālik is that the distribution among these categories is left to the judgment of the imam (ruler), so he may give it to some of them and not others. The position of al-Shāfiʿī is that it must be divided equally among all these categories.

The scholars differed over whether the faqīr (poor) is in greater need than the miskīn (needy), or the reverse. It was said that they are equal. It was also said that the faqīr is one who asks people and whose condition is known, while the miskīn is not like that.

﴿And those who work on them﴾: that is, those who collect the zakat and distribute it.

﴿And those whose hearts are to be reconciled﴾: these are unbelievers who are given in order to encourage them toward Islam. It was also said that they are Muslims who are given so that their faith may be firmly established. The scholars differed over whether this ruling remains in force or has lapsed because they are no longer needed.

﴿And for the freeing of slaves﴾: that is, slaves who are bought and freed.

﴿And those in debt﴾: that is, one who has a debt upon him. It is a condition that he must have incurred the debt for something other than corruption or extravagance.

﴿And in the cause of Allah﴾: that is, jihad. Those who engage in jihad are given from it, and weapons of war may be bought with it. The scholars differed over whether it may be spent on building city walls and constructing navies.

﴿And the wayfarer﴾: he is the traveller who is in need.

﴿An obligation﴾: that is, a binding right that is praiseworthy. It is in the accusative (naṣb) as a verbal noun (mafʿūl muṭlaq, an absolute object, i.e., a noun from the same root as the verb, used to emphasize or specify it).

If it is asked: why was the mention of the recipients of zakat placed within the mention of the hypocrites? The answer is that the restriction of the recipients of zakat to those categories was made in order to cut off the hypocrites' hope of receiving it. Thus this verse is connected in meaning to His saying: ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the ṣadaqāt﴾, and the rest of the verse.

﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet﴾: that is, among the hypocrites, and their harming of the Prophet (ﷺ) by words and deeds.

﴿And they say: he is an ear﴾: that is, he hears everything that is said to him and believes it. It is said that the one who uttered this statement was Nabtal ibn al-Ḥārith, who was one of the rebellious hypocrites. It was also said that it was ʿAttāb ibn Qushayr.

﴿Say: an ear of good for you﴾: that is, he hears what is good and true.

﴿And he believes in the believers﴾: that is, he gives them credence. It is said: "I believed you (āmantu laka)" when one means "I accepted what you said as true." For this reason this verb is followed by the preposition "ilā" (to/for), whereas the verb "yu'minu" in "believes in Allah" is followed by "bi-" (in).

﴿And mercy﴾: with the nominative (rafʿ) it is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon "ear", and with the genitive (khafḍ) it is a conjunction upon "of good".

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 9, verses 66–68:

﴿If We pardon a group among you﴾ A man among them named Makhshin repented and died as a martyr. ﴿Some of them are from others﴾ A negation that they are among the believers. ﴿And they withhold their hands﴾ A metaphor for miserliness. ﴿They forgot Allah﴾ That is, they neglected His remembrance. ﴿So He made them forget themselves﴾ He abandoned them from His mercy and His bounty. ﴿Allah has promised the hypocrites﴾ The original usage with regard to evil is to say "awʿada" (threatened), and it is only said "waʿada" (promised) when the evil is stated explicitly. ﴿And the disbelievers﴾ meaning those who openly declare disbelief.

(As for) "like those before you": this is addressed to the hypocrites. The kaf (ك) is in the accusative position, and the meaning is: "you did the same as the deeds of those before you." Or it is in the position of the predicate of a subject, with the implied meaning: "you are like those before you."

"And you engaged in discourse" (وَخُضْتُمْ): i.e., you mixed in, and it is a metaphor taken from wading (khawd) into water. It is only used for falsehood in speech.

"Like the manner in which they engaged" (كَٱلَّذِي خَاضُوۤاْ): its implied meaning is "like the engagement in which they engaged." It was also said: "like those who engaged," so here "alladhi" (the one), according to this view, carries the meaning of the plural.

﴿Has there not come to them﴾ (the verse): a warning to them with what befell the earlier nations. ﴿And the overturned cities﴾ means the cities of the people of Lot. ﴿With clear proofs﴾ means with miracles.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 9, verses 71–72:

﴿Some of them are allies of others.﴾ This is in contrast to His saying, "The hypocrites, men and women, are of one another" (Q. 9:67), but He singled out the believers with the attribute of being allies (awliya').

﴿Gardens of perpetual residence (Jannat 'Adn)﴾ It has been said: 'Adn is the city of Paradise and its greatest part. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is a proper name.

﴿And the good pleasure of Allah is greater﴾ meaning: the good pleasure of Allah is greater than everything mentioned. This is the meaning of what is mentioned in the hadith: "Indeed Allah, may He be exalted, says to the people of Paradise: 'Do you wish for anything more that I may give you?' They say: 'O our Lord, what could You give us more?' He says: 'My good pleasure, so I shall never be displeased with you forever.'"

ﷺ

"Strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites" (﴿jāhid al-kuffāra wa'l-munāfiqīn﴾). Jihad against the disbelievers is with the sword, and jihad against the hypocrites is with the tongue, so long as nothing appears from them that indicates their disbelief. If such a thing does appear from them, then their ruling is the ruling of the zindiq (one who conceals disbelief while outwardly professing Islam), and scholars have differed over whether he is to be killed or not. "And be harsh with them" (﴿wa'ghlud ʿalayhim﴾). Ghilẓa (harshness, sternness) is the opposite of mercy and tenderness, and it may be expressed through speech, through action, and otherwise.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 9, verse 74:

﴿They swear by Allah that they did not say [it]﴾. It was revealed concerning al-Jullas ibn Suwayd, for he said: "If what Muhammad says is true, then we are worse than donkeys." This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), so he recited it to him, and he swore that he had not said it. ﴿And they have certainly uttered the word of disbelief﴾, meaning what preceded from the statement of al-Jullas, because that implies denial. ﴿And they disbelieved after their Islam﴾. He did not say "after their faith," because they used to say with their tongues "We believe," while faith had not entered their hearts. ﴿And they planned what they did not attain﴾. They are al-Jullas, [planning] to kill the one who conveyed that statement about him. It was also said: they planned to kill the Prophet (ﷺ). It was also said: the verse was revealed concerning Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, and the word of disbelief he uttered was his saying: "Fatten your dog, and it will devour you." His planning what he did not attain was his saying: ﴿If we return to Medina, the more honorable will surely expel the more humble from it﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. ﴿And they resent only that Allah enriched them﴾, i.e., they found fault only in the wealth which they should have been thankful for. This applies to al-Jullas, or to Abdullah ibn Ubayy. ﴿So if they repent﴾: Allah opened for them the door of repentance, so al-Jullas repented and his condition became good.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 9, verses 75–77:

﴿وَمِنْهُمْ مَّنْ عَٰهَدَ ٱللَّهَ﴾ [And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah] — the verse was revealed concerning Tha'labah ibn Hatib. The reason was that he said, "O Messenger of Allah, pray to Allah that He makes my wealth increase." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him, "A little that you are able to thank for is better than a lot that you cannot bear." He kept repeating it to him until he (the Prophet) prayed for him, and his wealth increased. He became preoccupied with it until he abandoned the prayers. Then he refused to pay the zakat, so the verse was revealed about him. He brought his zakat to the Prophet (ﷺ), but he turned away from him and did not accept it from him, and said, "Allah has commanded me not to accept your zakat." Then Abu Bakr, Umar, and Uthman did not accept it from him either.

﴿بَخِلُواْ بِهِ﴾ [they were stingy with it] — an indication of his refusal to pay zakat.

﴿فَأَعْقَبَهُمْ نِفَاقاً﴾ [So He caused them to follow it with hypocrisy] — as a punishment for disobedience, with something worse than it.

﴿إِلَىٰ يَوْمِ يَلْقَوْنَهُ﴾ [until the Day they meet Him] — it is a judgment that they will die in hypocrisy.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 9, verse 79:

﴿Those who find fault with the volunteers among the believers in charity⟩ was revealed concerning the hypocrites when ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf gave four thousand (dirhams) in charity, and they said: "This is nothing but showing off." The original form of al-mutawwiʿin is al-mutatawwiʿin (those who volunteer beyond what is obligatory), and what is meant here is one who gives a great deal in charity. ﴿And those who find nothing to give except their effort⟩ are those who are able only to give a little, so they give that. It was revealed concerning Abu ʿAqil, who gave a sa' of dates, and the hypocrites said: "Surely God has no need of this man's charity." ﴿So they ridicule them⟩, that is, they belittle them. ﴿God will ridicule them⟩: this is the naming of the punishment by the name of the sin.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 9, verse 80:

﴿Ask forgiveness for them, or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾ It may bear two meanings. The first: its wording is a command, but its meaning is a condition, and the meaning is: "Whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them, Allah will never forgive them," as came in Surat al-Munafiqun. The second: that it is an option (takhyir), as if He said: "If you wish, ask forgiveness for them, and if you wish, do not ask forgiveness for them." Then Allah informed him that He would not forgive them. This second meaning is the more preferred (arjah), due to the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Allah gave me the choice and I chose," and that was when Umar said: "Will you pray over Abdullah ibn Ubayy, when Allah has forbidden you to pray over him?" ﴿seventy times﴾ He mentioned it as an illustration of a large number.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 9, verse 81–82:

﴿فَرِحَ ٱلْمُخَلَّفُونَ﴾ ("Those who were left behind rejoiced"), i.e., those whom God left behind from Badr and kept sitting away from it. In this there is belittling and blame for them, and for this reason it does not say "al-mutakhallifun." ﴿بِمَقْعَدِهِمْ﴾ ("in their sitting") means in their staying behind, ﴿خِلَٰفَ رَسُولِ ٱللَّهِ﴾ ("against the Messenger of God") means after him, when he set out for Tabuk. Thus "khilaf" in this reading is a adverbial of place (zarf). It was also said that it is a verbal noun from "khalafa," and on this reading it is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlih).

﴿وَقَالُواْ لاَ تَنفِرُواْ فِي ٱلْحَرِّ﴾ ("And they said: Do not go forth in this heat"). The one who uttered this statement was a man from the Banu Salamah who found the journey to Tabuk in the heat difficult. ﴿فَلْيَضْحَكُواْ قَلِيلاً وَلْيَبْكُواْ كَثِيراً﴾ ("So let them laugh a little and let them weep much") is a command in the sense of a statement: their little laughter is in the world for the duration of their stay in it, and their much weeping is in the Hereafter. It was also said that it is in the sense of a command, meaning they ought to be: laughing little and weeping much in the world for what they have fallen into.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 9, verse 83:

﴿To a group of them﴾. He did not say "to them" because some of them repented of hypocrisy and regretted staying behind. ﴿You will never go out with Me, ever﴾ as a punishment for them, carrying disgrace and rebuke. ﴿The first time﴾, meaning in the expedition of Tabuk. ﴿So sit with those who remain behind﴾, that is, with those who sit out, namely the women and the children.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 9, verse 84:

﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died, ever, nor stand at his grave.﴾ It was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, and the Prophet's (ﷺ) prayer over him when he died. It is narrated that he (ﷺ) did pray over him, and then the verse was revealed. It is also narrated that when the Prophet (ﷺ) stepped forward to pray over him, Jibril came to him, pulled his garment, and recited to him ﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died, ever⁠﻿...﴾ the verse, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) turned away and did not pray over him.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 9, verses 86–90:

﴿And when a surah is sent down﴾. It is said: it means Bara'ah (al-Tawbah, the surah of Repentance), but the stronger view is that it is general in meaning. ﴿That believe﴾: here *an* is explanatory (*mufassirah*). ﴿The people of means among them ask your permission﴾, i.e., those who have wealth and abundant property. ﴿But the Messenger﴾ and the rest of the verse, i.e., even if these people stay behind, the Messenger and those with him have striven. ﴿The good things﴾ encompass the benefits of both abodes. It is said that they are the wide-eyed maidens (*al-hur al-'in*), based on His saying: "good and beautiful ones" (*khayrat hisan*). ﴿And those who make excuses came﴾: they are *al-mu'tadhirun*, the ones who offer excuses. Then the *ta'* was assimilated into the *dhal*, and its vowel was transferred to the *'ayn*, so the word became *al-mu'adhdhirun* (المُعَذِّرُونَ). Scholars differed over whether they were truthful or lying in their excuses. It is also said that they are *al-maqsurun* (المَقصِّرون), from *'udhira fi al-amr* (عُذِرَ فِي الأَمْرِ), meaning one fell short in a matter and found no excuse for it; on this view, its measure is *al-mif'alun*. It is narrated that it was revealed concerning a group from Ghifar. ﴿And those who lied to Allah and His Messenger sat back﴾: they are a group who neither struggled nor offered excuses for their staying behind, so they lied in their claim of faith. ﴿Those of them who disbelieved will be struck﴾, i.e., of those who offered excuses.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 9, verses 106–107:

﴿And others are deferred to the command of Allah﴾. It is said: they are the three who stayed behind until Allah accepted their repentance. It is also said: they are those who built the Mosque of Harm. The word is read *murjawna* and *murji'un*, with and without the hamza, and both are dialectal forms (lughatan) meaning "delay" (al-ta'khir). ﴿And those who took a mosque﴾: it is read *alladhina* without the waw, as a qualifier (sifah) of *wa-akharuna murjawna*, or with the implied sense "those who". This reading accords with the view of those who said that the ones deferred to Allah's command are the people of the Mosque of Harm. It is also read *wa-alladhina* with the waw, as a conjunction (ataf) upon *akharuna murjawna*, and this reading accords with the view of those who said that the deferred ones are the three who stayed behind. ﴿For harm and disbelief﴾: the Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf among the Ansar had built the Mosque of Quba', and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to come to it and pray in it. Their people, the Banu Ghanm ibn 'Awf and the Banu Salim ibn 'Awf, envied them for this, so they built another mosque adjacent to it in order to cut people off from praying in the Mosque of Quba'. This is the harm they intended. They asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to come to it and pray for them there, so Allah revealed this verse concerning him. ﴿And to cause division among the believers﴾: they intended that the believers would disperse from the Mosque of Quba'. ﴿And as a station of observation for those who had warred against Allah and His Messenger before﴾: that is, a waiting place for one who had warred against Allah and His Messenger. This was Abu 'Amir the monk, whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) named "the Wicked". He was from the people of Madinah, and when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arrived there, he openly declared disbelief and hypocrisy. Then he went out to Makkah and instigated the confederates from among the polytheists. When Makkah was conquered, he went out to al-Ta'if, and when the people of al-Ta'if embraced Islam, he went out to Syria to seek help from the Caesar, and he died there. The people of the Mosque of Harm used to say: "When Abu 'Amir comes to Madinah, he will pray in this mosque." The reference in His words "before" is to what the confederates did to him. ﴿And they will surely swear, "We intended nothing but goodness"﴾: that is, the good outcome, which is prayer and the remembrance of Allah. Allah then refuted them in this claim.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 9, verses 113–114:

It is said that this became clear to him through his father's death in disbelief, and it is said that it was because he was forbidden to seek forgiveness for him. ﴿Indeed, Abraham was most tender-hearted and forbearing﴾ (la-awwah). It is said: one who supplicates much; it is said: one who is certain; it is said: a jurist; it is said: one who remembers Allah much; it is said: one who sighs much out of fear of Allah.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil, "The Facilitation") on surah 9, verses 118–119:**

﴿And upon the three who were left behind﴾: they were Ka'b ibn Malik, Hilal ibn Umayya, and Murara ibn al-Rabi'. They stayed behind from the expedition to Tabuk without any excuse, and not out of hypocrisy or any intention of opposition. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned, he was displeased with them and commanded that no one speak to them, and he ordered them to keep away from their wives. They remained in that state for a period until Allah revealed their repentance. Their story has been related in al-Bukhari, Muslim, and the sira (biographies of the Prophet). The meaning of "were left behind" here is: left behind from the expedition.

Ka'b ibn Malik said that its meaning is: they were left behind from accepting the harm, and not that they were left behind from the military campaign. What strengthens this is that He set a limit for their being left behind: ﴿when the earth became constricted for them﴾, which is an expression of the grief and fear of Allah that befell them. ﴿Then He turned to them in forgiveness so that they might repent﴾, meaning: He brought them back so that they would remain steadfast in repentance. ﴿And be with the truthful﴾: this may mean truthfulness of the tongue, since these three had told the truth and did not offer excuses through lies, so Allah benefited them by that. It may also mean something more general than truthfulness of the tongue, namely truthfulness in statements, actions, intentions, and resolves. By "the truthful" are meant the Muhajirun (Emigrants), based on Allah's words in surah al-Hashr: "for the poor Emigrants … it is they who are the truthful." Abu Bakr al-Siddiq used this verse as evidence against the Ansar on the day of Saqifa, saying: "We are the truthful, and Allah has commanded you to be with us," meaning: to follow us.

﴿It was not for the people of Madinah﴾ and so on, the verse: a rebuke for those who stayed behind from the expedition of Tabuk, from among the people of Yathrib and the Arab tribes around them. ﴿Nor should they prefer themselves over His self﴾, meaning: they should not refrain from undertaking the hardships that he (ﷺ) bore. ﴿That is because they will not be afflicted﴾: an explanation of why staying behind is not permissible. ﴿Thirst﴾, meaning thirst. ﴿Nor fatigue﴾, meaning exhaustion. ﴿Nor hunger﴾, meaning hunger. ﴿Nor do they tread﴾, meaning with their feet or with their mounts. ﴿Nor do they inflict upon an enemy any infliction﴾: a general statement covering everything that afflicts the disbelievers.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 9, verse 122:

﴿And it is not for the believers to go forth all together.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: This verse concerns the dispatching of detachments for military expeditions and the sariyyas (small raiding parties): that is, it is not appropriate for all the believers to set out in the sariyyas. Such a departure is obligatory only when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ himself goes out. That is why, in the preceding verse, He rebuked them for remaining behind from him. So the first verse concerns going out with him ﷺ, and this verse concerns the sariyyas that he ﷺ would dispatch. It is also said: it abrogates (naskh) every command that came requiring all to go forth, and so it is evidence that jihad is a collective obligation (fard kifaya) and not an individual obligation (fard ʿayn). It is also said: it concerns the seeking of knowledge, and its meaning is that the journey in pursuit of knowledge is not obligatory upon everyone, but upon some, because it is a collective obligation. ﴿Why should not a company from every group of them go forth?﴾ This is an exhortation (tahdid) for some of the believers to go forth for jihad or for the seeking of knowledge. ﴿That they may gain understanding in the religion.﴾ If we say the verse concerns going out to seek knowledge, then the pronoun in "yatafaqqahu" (they may gain understanding) refers to the company that goes forth, that is, travels. Likewise the pronoun in "yundhiru" (they may warn) and in "raja'u" (they return) refers to them: that is, that they may teach their people when they return to them from the journey. If we say the verse concerns the sariyyas, then the pronoun in "yatafaqqahu" refers to the company that remains in Madina and does not go out with the sariyyas, whereas the pronoun in "raja'u" refers to the company that went out with the sariyyas. ﴿That they may be wary.﴾ The pronoun refers to the people.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 9, verse 123:

﴿Fight those of the disbelievers who are near to you﴾ He commands fighting the nearest and then the next nearest, in gradual order. It was also said: this is a reference to fighting the Byzantines (al-Rum) in al-Sham, because they were the nearest of the disbelievers to the land of the Arabs, and the land of the Arabs had by then been covered by Islam, while Iraq at that time was far away.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 9, verses 128–129:

﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves.﴾ He means the Prophet (ﷺ). The address is to the Arabs, or specifically to the Quraysh, meaning from your own tribe, so that you know his lineage, truthfulness and trustworthiness. Or the address is to all the children of Adam, meaning from your own kind. It is also read *min anfusikum* with a fatha on the *fa'* (*min anfasikum*), meaning from the most noble of you. ﴿Painful to him is your suffering (ʿanit)﴾: that is, your hardship weighs heavily on him. *Al-ʿanit* (hardship, distress; the term here means what harms them in their religion or in their worldly affairs). *ʿAzīz* is a description of the Messenger, and *mā ʿanittum* is the subject of *ʿazīz*. *Mā* here is either a verbal-source particle (*mā maṣdariyya*, meaning "your suffering" as a verbal noun), or *mā ʿanittum* is itself a verbal noun. *ʿAzīz* is the predicate placed before its subject, and the whole clause stands in the position of a description. ﴿Ardently desirous for you﴾: that is, desirous of your faith and your happiness. ﴿For the believers, compassionate and merciful﴾: Allah names him here with two of His names.

﴿But if they turn away, then say: Allah is sufficient for me﴾: that is, if they turn away from faith, then seek help from Allah, rely upon Him. It has been said that these two verses were revealed in Mecca.

﴿But if they turn away, then say: Allah is sufficient for me﴾: that is, if they turn away from faith, then seek help from Allah, rely upon Him. It has been said that these two verses were revealed in Mecca.
